anchors.fact: In 1740 Admiral Edward Vernon, commanding the Royal Navy's West Indies station, ordered that his sailors' daily rum ration, until then drunk neat, be issued mixed with water. That was the start of grog. His stated concern was the "pernicious custom" of the men drinking their allowance in drams, "often at once". Oxford gives the danger as men who had to climb high into the rigging. (F1, F2, F3; Oxford GROG pdf 951, SPIRITS IN THE MILITARY pdf 1868)
anchors.meaning: The no nobody else would say, said for the people who have to climb. That it cost him anything to say it isn't on record: signpost it.
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: A reality check · texture: In control

anchors.fact: Four parts water to one of rum (half a pint of rum to a quart of water), split into two servings a day rather than one. The ratio later changed (two to one from 1937 until 1970). (F4; C1)
anchors.meaning: He didn't take it away. He made it last: "one now, and one later." The rule is about pace, not punishment.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The best version of me · drawnToward: Peace

anchors.fact: The order let men who were thrifty buy lime and sugar (out of savings on their provisions) to make it more palatable, which effectively turned it into punch. Palatability was the stated reason. The scurvy benefit is Oxford's later observation, not Vernon's motive. (F5; C2: don't quote "husbandmen")
anchors.meaning: Inside the rule he left room for their own taste. Structure with room in it: scaffolding, not a cage.

anchors.fact: The order had the mixing done in a scuttled butt (Oxford's gloss: "a repurposed barrel half") and served out openly, so the men could be sure they weren't cheated of their full allowance. (F6. "On deck" and "the lieutenant of the watch" are secondary: wordorigins.org)
anchors.meaning: Authority done in plain sight. Anyone can check that the rule is fair.

anchors.fact: The daily tot, always mixed into grog, stayed a formal ritual (the bosun's call "Up spirits!"). When the last ration was issued, on 31 July 1970 ("Black Tot Day"), sailors held mock burials at sea and wore black armbands. (F9, F10; Oxford RUM, NAVY pdf 1701–1702)
anchors.meaning: **Our reading, signposted:** the rule they were handed became something they mourned. Grog was issued for 230 years (1740 → 1970, checked), though the measure itself was cut twice (1824, 1851) and the ratio changed: never "the same measure". Never claim that the 1740 sailors liked it or hated it (L1).
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My future self · drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: Our drink keeps Vernon's first proportion: one measure of rum to four of cold water (F4, 1740 only), with no ice. It's our build, not his recipe: the rum is navy-strength (a style today; the Navy's 54.5% dates from 1866, F11), and it's made as a still highball ("A Highball can be effervescent or still", *Codex* p. 201).
anchors.meaning: The measure is the Nanny's, and nothing melts behind anyone's back: the ratio poured is the ratio drunk (Tomás's physics). Fair, and seen to be fair, the way the cask was.

anchors.fact: Lime juice and a demerara syrup, half a measure each: the two things Vernon let the men buy to make it taste better (F5).
anchors.meaning: The room for someone else's taste, inside a fixed measure. It's fixed in the spec, never "to taste", because a free-for-all isn't this person.

anchors.fact: Sherry vinegar in the syrup. The *Flavor Matrix* lists sherry vinegar among the best pairings for cane syrup and molasses (pdf 240; the entry is about those syrups, not demerara sugar). Vinegar is "the only common food acid that is aromatic" (*LI* p. 59, pdf 63).
anchors.meaning: **Tomás's reading, kept or cut by Wren:** a little sharpness inside the sweetness, care that doesn't only soothe. No historical claim: Vernon's men never had it.

anchors.fact: Reportedly, Vernon wore a coat of grogram, a gum-stiffened waterproof cloth, was nicknamed "Old Grogram", and the drink took the name. Oxford says "reportedly" both times. (F7)
anchors.kind: name (legend; in the reading as "Legend has it", y2)
anchors.meaning: Told only as a legend ("Legend has it", reading v3 y2; changed from "the story goes" for lint). No anchor meaning rests on it. "Old Grog" (the reading's form) is the Abbey's wording (secondary); Oxford has "Old Grogram".

anchors.fact: Don the Beachcomber's Navy Grog (in print 1942: rum, grapefruit, honey) is a punch, not a grog. (F12)
anchors.meaning: Keeps us from calling any tiki "grog" ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Four of water to one of rum. The lime and the sugar are theirs.
cocktail.glassware: tumbler or highball glass (about 300 ml), no ice
method: Make the syrup ahead, an hour or a day before. Warm the sugar and water in a small pan, stirring, until the liquid turns clear. Don't let it boil. Take it off the heat, stir in the sherry vinegar, let it cool, and bottle it. It keeps for about two weeks in the fridge.
Put a jug of water in the fridge so it's properly cold.
Use the same jigger for everything. Pour one jigger of rum into the glass.
Add four jiggers of cold water.
Add half a jigger of lime juice and half a jigger of syrup, and stir a few times. No ice: as it melted, it would change the measure.
cocktail.name: Fair Measure

recipe.note: strong enough to still taste of rum at four to one

cocktail.tagline: You were never against the fun. You're why it lasts.

reading.epigraph: Most of this glass is plain water. In 1740, that was an order.
whoYouAre: It's late, everyone's having a good time, and you're the one who says "one more, then home." You're the one who checks what's left in the account before the trip gets booked, who asks for a text when they're home, who keeps the Sunday call going long after the others have let it slide. Some people hear a rule. It isn't one, not really. It's what keeps the good thing there tomorrow.

People call you the sensible one, and on worse nights, something less kind. It stings more than you show, because you were never against the fun. You're the reason there's any left in the morning. Everyone else gets to forget the time because you never do. And somewhere under the plans is a fear you wouldn't say out loud: that if you stopped holding it all, it would come apart, and it would be your fault for wanting one night off.
yours: In 1740, Admiral Edward Vernon, in command of the British ships in the West Indies, put a stop to the way his sailors took their daily rum: in drams, often all at once, with work waiting for them high in the rigging. From then on it was mixed with water, at first four parts to one, and served in two portions a day instead of one.

What I like is what he didn't do. The rum stayed. He let the men buy lime and sugar to make it taste better. And he had it mixed in the open, in a half-barrel, so nobody could think they'd been given short measure. Legend has it he was called Old Grog, after the stiff, gum-proofed coat he wore, and the drink took his name.

The ration outlived him by more than two centuries. When the navy poured its last one, in July 1970, sailors held mock burials and wore black armbands. I like to think some of what they were mourning was the order of it: the call of "Up spirits!", the measure, the hour, every day. That's how you hold a line. You don't take the good thing away. You make it last, you leave room for everyone's own taste, and you do it where everyone can see it's fair.

The cocktail I've crafted for you is his order made into a long drink, with something he never had. One jigger of a strong rum, bottled well above the usual strength so the rum isn't lost at four to one, and four jiggers of cold water, measured with the same jigger. Then half a jigger each of fresh lime and a demerara syrup made ahead. There's no ice, because ice would melt and quietly change the measure. What's poured is what's drunk. The thing I added is in the syrup: a splash of sherry vinegar, a vinegar made from sherry, which you can smell as well as taste. So even the sweet part, the part that's handed over, has a little sharpness in it. I don't think you can help that, and I wouldn't want you to.

Next time you set the limit, set it, and then let the rest be theirs to make. Don't check how they did it. Focus on enjoying the fun yourself. The taste was always theirs. It'll still hold, and you might even get that night off.
